newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hero or Hitler? Chubais stirs emotions in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Hero or Hitler? Chubais stirs emotions in Russia.

text.p: Anatoly Chubais' return to the government stirred a storm in the Russian media on Tuesday, with commentators variously labelling him the only hope for reforms and a villain comparable to Adolf Hitler.

But while they had no doubt that the former presidential aide would shake up the administration, they had few clues as to the exact nature of the far-reaching cabinet reshuffle now scheduled to follow his appointment.
President Boris Yeltsin issued a decree making Chubais first deputy prime minister on Friday evening, at the start of a three-day holiday to mark Womens' Day.
Breaking the silence again on Tuesday, the Kremlin ordered Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to carry out a full reorganisation of the government this week.
Newspapers meanwhile unleashed a flood of contradictory assessments of the appointment of Chubais, who is expected to be the driving force behind the new administration.
"For his friends he is a progressive reformer, for his enemies a red-haired embodiment of evil," said the liberal opposition daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
"However both are united in one thing, that the quiet and balanced life of the government ended on March 6," it added.
The hardline Sovietskaya Rossiya took the most extreme line, drawing "an historical parallel between him and...Adolf Hitler."
"Both dragged the people into monstrous experiments," it said, blaming Chubais for declines in the birthrate and life expectancy since market reforms began in 1991.
At the other end of the scale, the English-language Moscow Times daily noted that Chubais had an ambiguous image, but said in an editorial he was still the best hope for reforms.

Chubais had virtually ruled out a return to communism by transferring property into private hands and was largely responsible for taming inflation during his previous term in the government from 1991 to 1996, it said.
An accompanying commentary by political analyst Andrei Piontkovsky spelt out the doubts surrounding the appointment.
"Who is Chubais? An architect of reform or a high-level manager of the affairs of a financial oligarchy? This is his moment of truth," it said.
Other papers said the appointment showed that Yeltsin, elected to a second term last July on promises of an easier life for ordinary Russians, had turned his back on the electorate.

"Appointing him first deputy prime minister is to spit at public opinion," said the popular Moscow daily Moskovsky Komsomolets in a caustic front-page article, echoing the line taken by communist leaders last week.
It recalled that Yeltsin had fired Chubais in January 1996, blaming him for all the woes brought about by Russia's chaotic and crime-ridden reforms and asked "Has something changed?".
The paper said it was not just the communists who were against Chubais but liberals too, because of his controversial role at the helm of Russia's mass privatisation programme.

It underlined the main criticism levelled at Chubais -- that he allowed Russia's wealth to be channelled into the hands of a few -- with a photograph showing a leading businessman leaning over the 41-year-old reformer at a dinner.
The caption had the businessman telling Chubais: "I demand that the banquet continue!"

Nezavisimaya Gazeta said that Chubais' declared aim of reforming housing, communal services and pensions and fighting natural monopolies would necessitate getting rid of the "red directors" from the upper echelons of power.
"His aim is to turn the government into an obedient and pliant instrument of the ideas of the reformer-in-chief," it said, adding that he was unlikely to fill the government with his cronies.
